claim: Data were extracted from 433 intertidal sites between 74.8°S and 80.5°N.
source: We extracted data from 433 intertidal sites between 74.8°S and 80.5°N (Figure 1).
evidence: The manuscript explicitly states the number of sites and latitudinal range of the dataset.

claim: Only 11 sites were located at latitudes above 70°, south and north combined.
source: Only 11 sites were located at latitudes above 70°, south and north combined (Supplementary file 1).
evidence: The manuscript provides a specific count of high-latitude sites with reference to supplementary data.

claim: α-diversity peaked at mid-latitudes between 30 and 55°N in the northern hemisphere.
source: A generalized additive mixed effect model (GAMM) indicated a non-linear relationship among α-diversity and latitude in the northern hemisphere where α-diversity peaked at mid-latitudes between 30 and 55°N (﻿GAMM, edf = 2.005, p=0.023).
evidence: Statistical analysis (GAMM) with reported parameters supports this finding.

claim: No latitudinal scale environmental driver was significant in the northern hemisphere.
source: While no latitudinal scale environmental driver was significant (Table 1), α-diversity was similar in the tropical and Arctic regions (Figure 2).
evidence: Table 1 shows non-significant p-values for all environmental drivers in the northern hemisphere model.

claim: α-diversity was similar in the tropical and Arctic regions.
source: While no latitudinal scale environmental driver was significant (Table 1), α-diversity was similar in the tropical and Arctic regions (Figure 2).
evidence: Figure 2 shows comparable α-diversity values at low and high latitudes in the northern hemisphere.

claim: In the southern hemisphere, α-diversity was not related to any latitudinal scale environmental drivers.
source: In the southern hemisphere, a generalized linear mixed effect model (GLMM) indicated that α-diversity was not related to any latitudinal scale environmental drivers (Table 1), and displayed a linear latitudinal pattern with a non-significant slight decline at the highest latitude (﻿Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: Table 1 shows non-significant p-values for all environmental drivers in the southern hemisphere model.

claim: Southern hemisphere α-diversity displayed a linear latitudinal pattern with a non-significant slight decline at the highest latitude.
source: In the southern hemisphere, a generalized linear mixed effect model (GLMM) indicated that α-diversity was not related to any latitudinal scale environmental drivers (Table 1), and displayed a linear latitudinal pattern with a non-significant slight decline at the highest latitude (﻿Table 1; Figure 2).
evidence: Statistical analysis and Figure 2 show this pattern.

claim: There was no support for a tropical-to-polar decrease in α-diversity.
source: α-Diversity differed among hemispheres with a mid-latitudinal peak in the north, and a non-significant unimodal pattern in the south, but there was no support for a tropical-to-polar decrease in α-diversity.
evidence: The abstract summarizes the findings showing no classic latitudinal diversity gradient.

claim: Local-scale drivers significantly affected α-diversity.
source: Although global-scale drivers had no discernible effect, the local-scale drivers significantly affected α-diversity, and our results reveal that latitudinal diversity gradients are outweighed by local processes.
evidence: The abstract states that local-scale drivers had significant effects while global-scale drivers did not.

claim: Latitudinal diversity gradients are outweighed by local processes.
source: Although global-scale drivers had no discernible effect, the local-scale drivers significantly affected α-diversity, and our results reveal that latitudinal diversity gradients are outweighed by local processes.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this conclusion based on the analysis.

claim: Species richness of predators, grazers, and suspension feeders declined with latitude.
source: In contrast to α-diversity patterns, species richness of three functional groups (predators, grazers, and suspension feeders) declined with latitude, coinciding with an inverse gradient in algae.
evidence: The abstract explicitly states this finding for three functional groups.

claim: Algal species richness increased with latitude.
source: In contrast to α-diversity patterns, species richness of three functional groups (predators, grazers, and suspension feeders) declined with latitude, coinciding with an inverse gradient in algae.
evidence: The abstract states an inverse gradient in algae compared to the other functional groups.

claim: Polar and tropical intertidal data were sparse.
source: Polar and tropical intertidal data were sparse, and more sampling is required to improve knowledge of marine biodiversity.
evidence: The abstract explicitly acknowledges data limitations.

claim: A positive relationship was identified between α-diversity and salinity.
source: A positive relationship was identified between α-diversity and salinity and macroalgal cover (Figure 3a,c), with salinity having the strongest effect (R2 = 0.19, 95% CI = 4.82–8.52, Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis with reported R2 and confidence intervals supports this relationship.

claim: A positive relationship was identified between α-diversity and macroalgal cover.
source: A positive relationship was identified between α-diversity and salinity and macroalgal cover (Figure 3a,c), with salinity having the strongest effect (R2 = 0.19, 95% CI = 4.82–8.52, Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical analysis and figures support this relationship.

claim: Salinity had the strongest effect on α-diversity among local-scale drivers (R2 = 0.19, 95% CI = 4.82–8.52).
source: A positive relationship was identified between α-diversity and salinity and macroalgal cover (Figure 3a,c), with salinity having the strongest effect (R2 = 0.19, 95% CI = 4.82–8.52, Figure 4).
evidence: Statistical parameters are provided showing the effect size.

claim: Wave exposure had a negative effect on α-diversity.
source: Wave exposure and ice scour had negative effects on α-diversity (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: The text and Figure 3 show this negative relationship.

claim: Ice scour had a negative effect on α-diversity.
source: Wave exposure and ice scour had negative effects on α-diversity (Figure 3b,d).
evidence: The text and Figure 3 show this negative relationship.

claim: High levels of wave exposure were necessary to affect levels of α-diversity.
source: The non-linear relationship between wave exposure and α-diversity showed that high levels of wave exposure were necessary to affect levels of α-diversity (Figure 3b).
evidence: The non-linear relationship shown in Figure 3b demonstrates this threshold effect.

claim: Fewer species inhabited ice-scoured shores compared to ice-free shores (95% CI = −0.57 – −0.23).
source: Fewer species inhabited ice-scoured shores compared to ice-free shores (95% CI = −0.57 – −0.23, Table 2), although the model only explained around 5% (R2 = 0.05) of the variation due to large differences in the number of species on both ice-scoured and ice-free shores (Figure 3c).
evidence: Statistical analysis with confidence intervals supports this finding.

claim: The ice scour model only explained around 5% (R2 = 0.05) of the variation in α-diversity.
source: Fewer species inhabited ice-scoured shores compared to ice-free shores (95% CI = −0.57 – −0.23, Table 2), although the model only explained around 5% (R2 = 0.05) of the variation due to large differences in the number of species on both ice-scoured and ice-free shores (Figure 3c).
evidence: The R2 value is explicitly reported.

claim: Predators, grazers, and suspension feeders declined with latitude in both hemispheres.
source: Four studied functional groups (algae, grazers, predators, and suspension feeders) displayed different latitudinal patterns (Figure 5). Predators, grazers, and suspension feeders declined with latitude in both hemispheres, coinciding with an increase in algal ﻿richness (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows these patterns across latitudes.

claim: Algal richness increased with latitude.
source: Predators, grazers, and suspension feeders declined with latitude in both hemispheres, coinciding with an increase in algal ﻿richness (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows this inverse pattern.

claim: The relative distribution of functional groups changed faster across latitudes in the southern hemisphere than in the northern hemisphere.
source: In general, the relative distribution of the functional groups changed faster across latitudes in the southern hemisphere where rapid changes were observed around 20°S, while northern hemisphere communities were more consistent from 25 to 60°N (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows different rates of change between hemispheres.

claim: Rapid changes in functional group distribution were observed around 20°S in the southern hemisphere.
source: In general, the relative distribution of the functional groups changed faster across latitudes in the southern hemisphere where rapid changes were observed around 20°S, while northern hemisphere communities were more consistent from 25 to 60°N (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows this pattern.

claim: Northern hemisphere communities were more consistent from 25 to 60°N.
source: In general, the relative distribution of the functional groups changed faster across latitudes in the southern hemisphere where rapid changes were observed around 20°S, while northern hemisphere communities were more consistent from 25 to 60°N (Figure 5).
evidence: Figure 5 shows this pattern.

claim: No data were available for functional groups at latitudes 15–25°N.
source: We were unable to describe functional groups at latitudes 15–25°N as no data were available (indicated as white bars in Figure 5).
evidence: The text explicitly states this data gap, which is shown in Figure 5.

claim: In the southern hemisphere, predators and grazers together formed 6.9% (±6.6 s.d.) of species between 20 and 55°S.
source: In the southern hemisphere, the proportion of predators and grazers declined beyond around 20°S, together forming 6.9% (±6.6 s.d.) of species accounted for between 20 and 55°S, but constituting 18.3% (±15.1 s.d.) of species in communities at latitudes less than 20°S (Figure 5).
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: In the southern hemisphere, predators and grazers constituted 18.3% (±15.1 s.d.) of species at latitudes less than 20°S.
source: In the southern hemisphere, the proportion of predators and grazers declined beyond around 20°S, together forming 6.9% (±6.6 s.d.) of species accounted for between 20 and 55°S, but constituting 18.3% (±15.1 s.d.) of species in communities at latitudes less than 20°S (Figure 5).
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: Suspension feeders constituted 34.6% (±9.6 s.d.) of species between 20 and 45°S in the southern hemisphere.
source: Suspension feeders were common in low- to mid-latitudes, constituting 34.6% (±9.6 s.d.) of the species present between 20 and 45°S (Figure 5).
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: In the northern hemisphere, predators accounted on average for 18.2% (±5.8 s.d.) of populations from 0 to 60°N.
source: In the northern hemisphere, predators were abundant at low- and mid-latitudes, accounting on average for 18.2% (±5.8 s.d.) of the populations from 0 to 60°N, before declining to 4.7% (±4.1 s.d.) at high latitudes between 61 and 80°N.
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: In the northern hemisphere, predators declined to 4.7% (±4.1 s.d.) at high latitudes between 61 and 80°N.
source: In the northern hemisphere, predators were abundant at low- and mid-latitudes, accounting on average for 18.2% (±5.8 s.d.) of the populations from 0 to 60°N, before declining to 4.7% (±4.1 s.d.) at high latitudes between 61 and 80°N.
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: Grazers stabilized at 25.4% (±6.4 s.d.) across 25°–80°N in the northern hemisphere.
source: The number of grazers decreased markedly from around 15°N, but stabilized at 25.4% (±6.4 s.d.) across 25°–80°N (Figure 5).
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: Suspension feeders decreased to 21.4% (±1.8 s.d.) at high latitudes between 60 and 80°N in the northern hemisphere.
source: Suspension feeders were the dominant functional group on shores in the northern hemisphere, especially between 25 and 60°N, but decreased to 21.4% (±1.8 s.d.) at high latitudes between 60 and 80°N (Figure 5).
evidence: Specific percentages and standard deviations are provided from the data analysis.

claim: At the highest latitudes in both hemispheres, suspension feeders were absent and only a few predators were present, while grazers and algae dominated.
source: In both hemispheres, the assemblage composition at the highest latitudes was substantially different from elsewhere; on these high polar shores, suspension feeders were absent and only a few predators were present, while grazers and algae dominated.
evidence: The text explicitly describes the functional group composition at high latitudes.

claim: 44% (n = 193) of all studies were from mid-latitude rocky shores in Europe and North America between 24 and 60°N.
source: While we show data from 11 sites at latitudes above 70° (south and north combined), 44% (n = 193) of all studies were from mid-latitude rocky shores in Europe and North America between 24 and 60°N.
evidence: Specific percentages and counts are provided describing the sampling distribution.

claim: The latitudinal diversity gradient has been recognized for centuries.
source: The latitudinal diversity gradient in species richness across ecosystems and various functional groups has been a major research topic that has intrigued scientists since at least Darwin, 1859 and Wallace, 1878.
evidence: Historical citations to Darwin and Wallace support this claim.

claim: Ecological and physical hypotheses dominate discussions of latitudinal diversity gradients and include drivers such as habitat area, stability, speciation rates, energy availability, and temperature.
source: Ecological and physical hypotheses dominate the discussions and include drivers such as habitat area, stability, speciation rates, energy availability, and temperature (Willig et al., 2003; Clarke and Gaston, 2006; Edgar et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations to relevant literature support this claim about the hypotheses.

claim: Unimodal, bimodal, and inverse gradients emerge across clades, habitats, and latitudes.
source: However, the geographic, functional, and taxonomic generality of latitudinal diversity gradients remain lively debated as unimodal, bimodal, and inverse gradients emerge across clades, habitats, and latitudes (Rivadeneira et al., 2002; Waller, 2008; Chaudhary et al., 2016; Kinlock et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations to studies showing different gradient patterns support this claim.

claim: Latitudinal gradients in some marine groups have been shown to be closely related to water temperature.
source: In the marine realm, latitudinal gradients in some groups have ﻿been shown to be closely related to oceanographic covariates, such as water temperature (Roy et al., 2000), yet mammal richness peaks at high latitudes (Grady et al., 2019), and more species have been reported from polar soft-sediment habitats than at many lower latitudes (Vause et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to Roy et al., 2000 supports this claim.

claim: Marine mammal richness peaks at high latitudes.
source: In the marine realm, latitudinal gradients in some groups have ﻿been shown to be closely related to oceanographic covariates, such as water temperature (Roy et al., 2000), yet mammal richness peaks at high latitudes (Grady et al., 2019), and more species have been reported from polar soft-sediment habitats than at many lower latitudes (Vause et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to Grady et al., 2019 supports this claim.

claim: More species have been reported from polar soft-sediment habitats than at many lower latitudes.
source: In the marine realm, latitudinal gradients in some groups have ﻿been shown to be closely related to oceanographic covariates, such as water temperature (Roy et al., 2000), yet mammal richness peaks at high latitudes (Grady et al., 2019), and more species have been reported from polar soft-sediment habitats than at many lower latitudes (Vause et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to Vause et al., 2019 supports this claim.

claim: Macroalgal canopies shelter understory species from environmental stress.
source: Macroalgal canopies shelter understory species from environmental stress (Krause-Jensen et al., 2016; Sejr et al., 2021), creating protective microhabitats that increase environmental heterogeneity and biodiversity, thereby maintaining a diversified understory assemblages (Bulleri et al., 2002; Watt and Scrosati, 2013; Piazzi et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the ecological role of macroalgal canopies.

claim: Macroalgal canopies create protective microhabitats that increase environmental heterogeneity and biodiversity.
source: Macroalgal canopies shelter understory species from environmental stress (Krause-Jensen et al., 2016; Sejr et al., 2021), creating protective microhabitats that increase environmental heterogeneity and biodiversity, thereby maintaining a diversified understory assemblages (Bulleri et al., 2002; Watt and Scrosati, 2013; Piazzi et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the ecological effects of canopies.

claim: Suspension feeders are important benthic-pelagic energy couplers.
source: Suspension feeders are important benthic-pelagic energy couplers (Gili and Coma, 1998), and predation is widely accepted as a central structuring process in the composition and abundance of species (Vermeij, 1987; Stanley, 2008).
evidence: Citation to Gili and Coma, 1998 supports this claim.

claim: Predation is widely accepted as a central structuring process in the composition and abundance of species.
source: Suspension feeders are important benthic-pelagic energy couplers (Gili and Coma, 1998), and predation is widely accepted as a central structuring process in the composition and abundance of species (Vermeij, 1987; Stanley, 2008).
evidence: Citations to Vermeij, 1987 and Stanley, 2008 support this claim.

claim: Suspension feeders dominate benthic systems in fully marine environments at high latitudes.
source: Latitudinal studies have shown that suspension feeders dominate benthic systems in fully marine environments at high latitudes (Gili and Coma, 1998; De Broyer et al., 2014), while diversity of coastal macroalgae peaks at mid-latitudes (Keith et al., 2014), and predation pressure decreases with latitude and depth from shallow shelves to deep oceans (Taylor and Taylor, 1977; Harper and Peck, 2016).
evidence: Citations support this claim about suspension feeder dominance at high latitudes.

claim: Diversity of coastal macroalgae peaks at mid-latitudes.
source: Latitudinal studies have shown that suspension feeders dominate benthic systems in fully marine environments at high latitudes (Gili and Coma, 1998; De Broyer et al., 2014), while diversity of coastal macroalgae peaks at mid-latitudes (Keith et al., 2014), and predation pressure decreases with latitude and depth from shallow shelves to deep oceans (Taylor and Taylor, 1977; Harper and Peck, 2016).
evidence: Citation to Keith et al., 2014 supports this claim.

claim: Predation pressure decreases with latitude and depth from shallow shelves to deep oceans.
source: Latitudinal studies have shown that suspension feeders dominate benthic systems in fully marine environments at high latitudes (Gili and Coma, 1998; De Broyer et al., 2014), while diversity of coastal macroalgae peaks at mid-latitudes (Keith et al., 2014), and predation pressure decreases with latitude and depth from shallow shelves to deep oceans (Taylor and Taylor, 1977; Harper and Peck, 2016).
evidence: Citations to Taylor and Taylor, 1977 and Harper and Peck, 2016 support this claim.

claim: Intertidal shores rank as one of the most studied marine habitats.
source: Intertidal shores rank as one of the most studied marine habitats and are often seen as harbingers for the effects of climate change and invasive species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about intertidal research.

claim: Intertidal shores are often seen as harbingers for the effects of climate change and invasive species.
source: Intertidal shores rank as one of the most studied marine habitats and are often seen as harbingers for the effects of climate change and invasive species.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the role of intertidal habitats in ecological research.

claim: Regional-scale intertidal studies have found richness gradients of gastropods along coastlines in the eastern Pacific Ocean.
source: Regional-scale intertidal studies have found richness gradients of gastropods along coastlines in the eastern Pacific Ocean (Rivadeneira et al., 2015; Fenberg and Rivadeneira, 2019).
evidence: Citations support this claim about regional gastropod gradients.

claim: No latitudinal diversity gradient of gastropods was found on a global scale across oceans.
source: However, no latitudinal diversity gradient of gastropods (Miloslavich et al., 2013) or macroalgae (Konar et al., 2010) was found on a global scale across oceans, and assemblage-wide studies have found missing (Blanchette et al., 2008; Cruz-Motta et al., 2010) or inverse (Griffiths and Waller, 2016) gradients.
evidence: Citation to Miloslavich et al., 2013 supports this claim.

claim: No latitudinal diversity gradient of macroalgae was found on a global scale across oceans.
source: However, no latitudinal diversity gradient of gastropods (Miloslavich et al., 2013) or macroalgae (Konar et al., 2010) was found on a global scale across oceans, and assemblage-wide studies have found missing (Blanchette et al., 2008; Cruz-Motta et al., 2010) or inverse (Griffiths and Waller, 2016) gradients.
evidence: Citation to Konar et al., 2010 supports this claim.

claim: Assemblage-wide studies have found missing or inverse latitudinal diversity gradients in intertidal systems.
source: However, no latitudinal diversity gradient of gastropods (Miloslavich et al., 2013) or macroalgae (Konar et al., 2010) was found on a global scale across oceans, and assemblage-wide studies have found missing (Blanchette et al., 2008; Cruz-Motta et al., 2010) or inverse (Griffiths and Waller, 2016) gradients.
evidence: Citations to multiple studies support this claim.

claim: High habitat heterogeneity creates environmental stress mosaics that are more important in shaping biological patterns than latitudinal environmental gradients.
source: For example, high habitat heterogeneity creates environmental stress mosaics that are more important in shaping biological patterns than latitudinal environmental gradients (Helmuth et al., 2006; Jurgens and Gaylord, 2018).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the importance of habitat heterogeneity.

claim: Only the extent of intertidal mud flats have been quantified on a large scale.
source: In fact, only the extent of intertidal mud flats have been quantified on a large scale (Murray et al., 2019).
evidence: Citation to Murray et al., 2019 supports this claim.

claim: In recent decades intertidal diversity data from both polar regions have advanced.
source: However, in recent decades intertidal diversity data from both polar regions have advanced (Weslawski et al., 2010; Griffiths and Waller, 2016; Thyrring et al., 2017; Thyrring et al., 2021; Peck, 2018), providing novel opportunities to study biodiversity patterns and variation in specific functional groups on a worldwide scale.
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about recent advances in polar intertidal research.

claim: Rocky shores and boulder fields represent the most studied intertidal habitats and are present in all oceans.
source: Therefore, to control for habitat effects, we specifically focus on rocky shores and boulder fields, as they represent the most studied intertidal habitats and are present in all oceans.
evidence: This is stated as justification for the study's focus.

claim: The study examined patterns in intertidal α-diversity and functional groups across 155° of latitude.
source: We aim to examine patterns in intertidal α-diversity and functional groups across 155° of latitude, and test the following hypotheses: (1) α-diversity decreases with increasing latitude, as evident in other ecosystems and (2) biodiversity is predicted by local-scale structuring processes rather than global-scale oceanographic features.
evidence: The text explicitly states the latitudinal range examined.

claim: Subtidal benthic habitats experience relatively homogenous environmental conditions across small-to-moderate spatial scales.
source: ﻿Subtidal benthic habitats experience relatively homogenous environmental conditions across small-to-moderate spatial scales, and large-scale latitudinal diversity gradients are therefore less impacted by local factors and reflect larger-scale changes in environmental conditions.
evidence: This is stated as a comparison to explain differences between subtidal and intertidal patterns.

claim: Decreasing water temperatures profoundly affect physiological performance of marine ectotherms.
source: For instance, decreasing water temperatures profoundly affect physiological performance of marine ectotherms (e.g., growth, reproduction and activity, muscle performance) and special adaptations are required to live in cold waters (Peck, 2016; Peck, 2018).
evidence: Citations to Peck, 2016 and Peck, 2018 support this claim.

claim: Special adaptations are required for marine ectotherms to live in cold waters.
source: For instance, decreasing water temperatures profoundly affect physiological performance of marine ectotherms (e.g., growth, reproduction and activity, muscle performance) and special adaptations are required to live in cold waters (Peck, 2016; Peck, 2018).
evidence: Citations to Peck, 2016 and Peck, 2018 support this claim.

claim: Latitudinal biodiversity gradients in ectotherms have been attributed to changes in water temperatures in subtidal habitats.
source: Latitudinal biodiversity gradients in ectotherms have, therefore, been attributed to changes in water temperatures in subtidal habitats (Roy et al., 2000; Edgar et al., 2017).
evidence: Citations support this claim about temperature effects on subtidal biodiversity gradients.

claim: Organisms inhabiting the intertidal do not conform to classic latitudinal diversity gradient patterns.
source: Our data run contrary to this and indicate that organisms inhabiting the intertidal do not conform to classic LDG patterns, or any of the correlated environmental drivers (e.g., water temperature).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's data analysis.

claim: The importance of microhabitats, biological interactions, and local physical parameters on intertidal community assemblage, density, and diversity has been studied extensively on rocky intertidal shores.
source: Indeed, the importance of microhabitats; biological interactions; and local physical parameters on intertidal community assemblage, density, and diversity has been studied extensively on rocky intertidal shores (Paine, 1974; Archambault and Bourget, 1996; Coleman et al., 2006; Scrosati and Heaven, 2007; Piazzi et al., 2018; Sejr et al., 2021), and high spatial variable in intertidal community coverage and structure between closely adjacent areas are well known (Underwood and Chapman, 1996; Benedetti-Cecchi and Cinelli, 1997; Sejr et al., 2021).
evidence: Multiple citations support this claim about the extensive research on local factors.

claim: High spatial variability in intertidal community coverage and structure between closely adjacent areas is well known.
source: Indeed, the importance of microhabitats; biological interactions; and local physical parameters on intertidal community assemblage, density, and diversity has been studied extensively on rocky intertidal shores (Paine, 1974; Archambault and Bourget, 1996; Coleman et al., 2006; Scrosati and Heaven, 2007; Piazzi et al., 2018; Sejr et al., 2021), and high spatial variable in intertidal community coverage and structure between closely adjacent areas are well known (Underwood and Chapman, 1996; Benedetti-Cecchi and Cinelli, 1997; Sejr et al., 2021).
evidence: Citations support this claim about spatial variability.

claim: Algal canopies provide food, predation refugium, and a moist understory environment where species sensitive to desiccation stress can survive during low tides.
source: For example, algal canopies provide food, predation refugium, and a moist understory environment where species sensitive to desiccation stress can survive during low tides (Dayton, 1975), thus the understory community may be rich and distinct from the surrounding open shoreline (Benedetti-Cecchi et al., 2001; Bulleri et al., 2002; Watt and Scrosati, 2013).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the ecological functions of algal canopies.

claim: The understory community under algal canopies may be rich and distinct from the surrounding open shoreline.
source: For example, algal canopies provide food, predation refugium, and a moist understory environment where species sensitive to desiccation stress can survive during low tides (Dayton, 1975), thus the understory community may be rich and distinct from the surrounding open shoreline (Benedetti-Cecchi et al., 2001; Bulleri et al., 2002; Watt and Scrosati, 2013).
evidence: Citations support this claim about understory communities.

claim: Canopies and surface topography shelter organisms from extreme air temperatures, thereby increasing local coverage and diversity.
source: Canopies and surface topography also shelter organisms from extreme air temperatures, thereby increasing local coverage and diversity, and facilitating recolonization of the substrate by secondary species (Blanchard and Bourget, 1999; Watt and Scrosati, 2013; Ørberg et al., 2018).
evidence: Citations support this claim about the protective effects of canopies.

claim: Wave exposure decreases diversity, especially at high latitude where floating ice is pushed on the shore by waves, amplifying the impacts of ice scour on exposed coastlines.
source: Moreover, wave exposure decreases diversity, especially at high latitude where floating ice is pushed on the shore by waves, amplifying the impacts of ice scour on exposed coastlines (Scrosati and Heaven, 2007).
evidence: Citation supports this claim about wave exposure effects.

claim: Low tides occurring in the tropics during the hottest time of the day are more harmful than low tides in the middle of the night.
source: Even wave splashing and low water timing (i.e., low tides occurring in the tropics during the hottest time of the day are more harmful than low tides in the middle of the night [Helmuth et al., 2002]) have been shown to be important.
evidence: Citation to Helmuth et al., 2002 supports this claim.

claim: The combined stress experienced by resident populations may roughly balance out across most latitudes and produce no clear gradient.
source: Thus, although the strength and direction of environmental stressors change across latitudes (i.e., from ice scour and extreme sub-zero temperature in polar regions to desiccation and acute heat stress in the tropics), the combined stress experienced by resident populations may roughly balance out across most latitudes and produce no clear gradient.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the discussion of multiple interacting stressors.

claim: α-diversity generally did not conform to latitudinal diversity gradient predictions for either the Atlantic or Pacific coast of South America.
source: In a recent study in South America, α-diversity generally did not conform to latitudinal diversity gradient predictions for either the Atlantic or Pacific coast (Cruz‐Motta et al., 2020), and we demonstrate similar patterns on a global scale.
evidence: Citation to Cruz‐Motta et al., 2020 supports this claim.

claim: In polar regions where glaciers or a persistent ice foot covers the intertidal, no communities are present.
source: In polar regions where glaciers or a persistent ice foot covers the intertidal, no communities are present (Dayton, 1990; Peck, 2018), and where the intertidal is characterized by a seasonal ice-foot formation, colonization is only possible during spring and summer (Barnes, 1999), although in these areas it is possible that a few species might persist in highly saline brine pools in winter (Clarke and Beaumont, 2020).
evidence: Citations support this claim about ice-covered intertidal zones.

claim: Where the intertidal is characterized by a seasonal ice-foot formation, colonization is only possible during spring and summer.
source: In polar regions where glaciers or a persistent ice foot covers the intertidal, no communities are present (Dayton, 1990; Peck, 2018), and where the intertidal is characterized by a seasonal ice-foot formation, colonization is only possible during spring and summer (Barnes, 1999), although in these areas it is possible that a few species might persist in highly saline brine pools in winter (Clarke and Beaumont, 2020).
evidence: Citation to Barnes, 1999 supports this claim.

claim: A few species might persist in highly saline brine pools in winter in areas with seasonal ice-foot formation.
source: In polar regions where glaciers or a persistent ice foot covers the intertidal, no communities are present (Dayton, 1990; Peck, 2018), and where the intertidal is characterized by a seasonal ice-foot formation, colonization is only possible during spring and summer (Barnes, 1999), although in these areas it is possible that a few species might persist in highly saline brine pools in winter (Clarke and Beaumont, 2020).
evidence: Citation to Clarke and Beaumont, 2020 supports this speculative claim.

claim: Future reduction of glaciers, ice shelves, and ice foots in polar regions will permit organisms to colonize the intertidal zone.
source: Any future reduction of glaciers, ice shelves, and ice foots in these regions will therefore permit organisms to colonize the intertidal zone (Węsławski et al., 2011; Kennicutt et al., 2014; Kennicutt et al., 2015; Kennicutt et al., 2019).
evidence: Citations support this prediction about future colonization.

claim: Reduction of ice in polar regions will result in increased biomass and α-diversity as is evident from the high Arctic.
source: This will result in increased biomass and α-diversity as is evident from the high Arctic (Weslawski et al., 2010; Kortsch et al., 2012; Thyrring et al., 2021).
